evidence: Cic. Arch. 23: incitāmentum perīculōrum et labōrum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: What urges someone on, with the genitive of what it urges to, or ad: Cicero’s glory is the incitāmentum for facing dangers and toil.

evidence: Cic. Rep. 1.3: ad hanc voluntātem ipsīus nātūrae stimulīs incitāmur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally an ox-goad; figuratively what drives one on (also, what torments: see stimulate).

evidence: Quint. 1.3.8: studium discendī voluntāte, quae cōgī nōn potest, cōnstat
terms.comment: The motivation that comes from within: studium discendī, the wish to learn. The same word is “study” and, of judges, “bias” (see bias).
A motive in the sense of the reason why someone acts (see reason). Traupman gives ratiō with the genitive, “the reason for”, which classically is the reckoning or principle behind something.

phrases.latin: studium discendī voluntāte, quae cōgī nōn potest, cōnstat
phrases.english: the wish to learn depends on willingness, and willingness cannot be forced
What was his motive in coming?
